To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) The tammar is a seasonal breeder with an annual cycle of reproductive activity that is regulated by photoperiod.
the prolactine pulse is the critical element that maintains the seasonal inhibition of the corpus luteum in the tammar.

the morning prolactin pulse in female tammers kept in an inhibiting photoperiod is the critical factor for maintenance of CL inhibition during seasonal quiescent, and that this inhibition is not due to the inhibitory photoperoid alone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the endocrine control of the seasonal breeding of the tammar wallaby, Macropus (Macropus) eugenii.
the endocrinology of reproduction in the tammar wallaby, Macropus, eugenii.
the endocrine regulation of the seasonal breeding cycle of the tammar wallaby (Macropus eugeniii).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prolactins are involved in the regulation of the reproductive function in the tammar and that prolactin plays an essential role in the seasonal quiescence of the CL of tammars.
the prolactine pulse is the critical signal in the maintenance of seasonal quiescence of the CL.
the morning pulse of prolactine maintains the seasonal quiescence of the corpus luteum of the tammar, and that this effect is mediated through the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the maintenance of seasonal quiescence of the CL is due to a combination of a photoperiodic signal (the short days) and a prolactin pulse, and that the photoperiodic effect is mediated by the prolactin.

the tammar has evolved a system whereby the CL of the quiescent female is inhibited by the prolactin surge and that the maintenance of the prolactin inhibition of the CL is achieved by the prolactonin pulse.
prolactin is the critical factor for the inhibition of the reproductive axis during seasonal quiesence in female tammar, and prolactin acts by inhibiting LH secretion.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the pulse of prolactine, present in female tammar wallabies kept in an inhibiting photoperiod and missing 5 days after the switch to a stimulatory one, was artificially preserved during stimulatory photodiodes (Experiments 1A and B) or abolished during the inhibitory photoperoid (Experiment 2).
the pulse of prolactine is the critical factor for maintaining the seasonal reproductive quiescence in tammar wallabies.
